newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nordics in tough joint position on alcohol imports.
newsitem.headline: Nordics in tough joint position on alcohol imports.

text.p: The EU's three Nordic members are taking a tough line in talks with the European Commission on phasing out rules which allow them to limit the amount of alcohol people may bring back home from elsewhere in the bloc.

Sweden, Finland and Denmark want to keep their restrictions on personal alcohol imports unchanged until at least 1999, Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen told reporters during the weekend European Union summit in Dublin.
A Swedish finance ministry official confirmed on Monday that Stockholm, Copenhagen and Helsinki would present such a joint negotiation position on the controversial issue.
"It is a way for the Nordic countries to show a united front," ministry official Carl Gustav Fernlund told the Swedish news agency in Stockholm.

However, this position seems unlikely to go down well with Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti who is pushing for an agreement to start phasing out the restrictions already in 1997 and a set date for when they would end altogether.

Denmark, Sweden and Finland all have exemptions from EU rules so that they can restrict imports of cheaper alcohol, but these will expire by the end of 1996 unless there is a new agreement -- at least according to the Commission.

The Commission wants the restrictions to end because it says they go against the internal market -- where goods are supposed to flow freely -- while the Nordics want to keep them because of health- and tax-reasons.
The issue is politically sensitive for the Nordic states which have a traditional policy of high taxes on alcohol as part of efforts to reduce excessive drinking.
It is also a question of fiscal importance. In Sweden, taxes on alcohol and tobacco bring in a total of 18 billion crowns annually in state revenue.
In a weekend interview with Finnish daily Ilta-Sanomat, Monti said Finland should start changing its rules already next year, allowing people to gradually bring home more alcohol and cigarettes.
"The Commission is, on its part, prepared to be flexible. But also Finland has to show that it is prepared to take steps towards normal EU practice," he was quoted as saying.

Monti underlined the need to agree on on a deadline for the abolishment of the restrictions. "Most important is that we agree on a definite and unquestionable date when the restrictions will be abolished," Monti said.

A compromise leading to a phasing out of the restrictions would gradually allow Swedes, Finns and Danes to bring in more alcohol while at the same giving the three Nordics time to prepare for the new rules, according to the Commission.
But as Nordic excise duties on alcohol are much higher than elsewhere in the EU, some fear individual alcohol imports would jump if the Nordics lost their right to restrict imports.
Sweden and Finland won the right to limit alcohol imports during the accession negotiations in 1994, linking this to a Danish deal struck two years earlier.
Under current rules, a Swede is allowed to take home up to one litre of spirits, five litres of wine and 15 litres of beer, much less than most other EU citizens.
